sections.preamble:
## Board and map The board is a hexagon of 91 hexes, and every map is identical for both players under a half-turn rotation. - **Labels.** Each hex has a letter (A to K) for its diagonal column and a number (1 to 11) for its row. The centre is F6. - **Bases.** Player A starts at B6 and Player B at J6, eight hexes apart. - **Blocked hexes.** 12 hexes are impassable. They create chokepoints. - **Nodes.** Each side has one Node two hexes from its Base and two more between three and five hexes out. The seventh Node is F6. - **Generation.** A seed picks the blocked hexes and Nodes for one half, and the engine rotates them onto the other half. It rejects any map whose playable hexes are not all connected. The same seed always gives the same map, so a match can be re-run or replayed exactly. ## Turn structure Both players plan from the same state at the same time, and neither sees the other's orders until the turn resolves. ```mermaid flowchart LR S["State for turn N
sent to both players"] --> A1["Player A plans
reads, scouts, simulates"] --> A2["A submits orders"] S --> B1["Player B plans
reads, scouts, simulates"] --> B2["B submits orders"] A2 --> E["Engine resolves
both sets together"] B2 --> E E -->|"becomes the state for turn N+1"| S ``` 1. The engine publishes the state for turn N. Each player receives only the part its visibility allows. 2. Each player plans privately: it reads the state, scouts, simulates and updates its notes. 3. Each player submits one final order set, with a stated intent and a prediction of the opponent's move. 4. Once both have submitted or timed out, the engine resolves the two order sets together. 5. The engine publishes the state for turn N+1. A slow player delays the resolution and gains nothing from it. The two players' model calls can run in parallel. ## Orders and action points Each player has 6 action points per turn, and unused points are lost. | Action | Cost | Effect | | --- | --- | --- | | Move | 1 | Send N troops from a hex you own to an adjacent playable hex | | Scout | 1 | Reveal one hex and its six neighbours, anywhere on the board | - **Splitting.** Several moves may leave one hex, as long as they total no more than the troops there at the start of the turn. - **One step.** Troops move one hex per turn. Troops that arrive this turn cannot move again until the next. - **Emptying a hex.** A hex stays yours when its last troop leaves. - **Invalid orders.** If a submission contains an order that breaks a rule, it is rejected with the reasons and the player may submit once more. In that final submission an invalid order is dropped, still costs its action point, and is logged as wasted. Simulating, and reading or writing notes, cost no action points. ## Resolution The engine applies both order sets in one fixed sequence, using whole numbers only. 1. **Validate.** Drop invalid orders and any beyond the action-point limit. 2. **Depart.** Remove moving troops from their source hexes. 3. **Clash on the edge.** If the players move across the same edge in opposite directions, the smaller force is destroyed and the larger loses the same number. 4. **Arrive.** Add the surviving troops to their destination hexes. 5. **Fight in the hex.** Where both players have troops, or one enters a hex the other owns, apply the combat rule below. 6. **Take neutral Nodes.** A force entering a neutral Node must exceed its garrison, and loses that many troops. A smaller force is destroyed and wears the garrison down by its own size. 7. **Set ownership.** A hex with surviving troops belongs to their player. A hex with none keeps its owner. 8. **Check for knockout.** A captured Base ends the match. 9. **Produce.** Each Base gains 2 troops and each owned Node gains 1. **Combat rule.** The owner of the hex adds the home bonus of 1 to its strength. The larger strength wins and loses troops equal to the smaller strength, and the home bonus absorbs the owner's first loss. On a tie the attackers are destroyed and the hex does not change hands. | Attackers | Defenders in a hex they own | Result | | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | 0 | Attack fails, hex holds | | 2 | 0 | Captured, 1 attacker left | | 4 | 3 | Attack fails, no defenders left, hex holds | | 5 | 3 | Captured, 1 attacker left | | 3 | 5 | Attack fails, 3 defenders left | If both players enter the same neutral hex, they fight each other first with no bonus, and the survivor then faces any garrison. ## Visibility and scouting A player sees its own hexes and every hex next to them, and the rest of the board is hidden. - **Always known.** The terrain of every hex (blocked, plain, Node or Base) and both players' scores. Base locations are therefore never hidden; only their troop counts are. - **Visible hexes.** Owner, troop count and garrison. - **Hidden hexes.** Terrain only. The engine does not report what was last seen there. - **Scouting.** One action point reveals a chosen hex and its six neighbours as they stood at the start of the turn. The result comes back at once, before orders are submitted. - **Turn report.** After each resolution a player is told about the fights and captures on hexes it could see. Remembering what it saw earlier is the player's job. That information is in its own conversation history and in whatever it chose to put in its notes. ## Scoring and match end The match ends after turn 25 or when a Base falls, and the higher score wins. - **Points.** A plain hex or a Base is worth 1 and a Node is worth 3. - **Supply.** Only hexes connected to your Base through a chain of your own hexes score. A region cut off from the Base scores nothing until it is reconnected, though its Nodes still produce troops. - **Knockout.** Capturing the enemy Base ends the match at once. It is recorded as 93 to 0 whatever the score at that moment, and the turn is logged. A strike at the Base is therefore a real alternative to taking hexes. - **Margin.** The result records the winner and the points difference. The margin is the main input to series statistics. - **Draws.** Equal scores are a draw. So is a turn on which both Bases fall. You are one of the two players in a game of Salient. You act only through the salient tools. The whole match is one conversation. Each turn you receive a message naming the turn. Everything from earlier turns stays in this conversation, so build a strategy and adjust it as the game goes. On turn 1, call get_rules once. It gives the constants and the map: every hex, its terrain and its neighbours. Each turn: 1. Call get_state. 2. Plan. You may scout (1 action point each) and simulate (up to 3 times). 3. Call submit_orders with your orders, your intent and your prediction of the enemy's move. If any order is invalid you are told why and may submit once more; that second submission is final. You have 12 tool calls a turn, not counting submit_orders. If you never submit, you pass the turn. You also have notes (read_notes, write_notes). Notes last for the whole match, even if the early conversation is summarised to save space. The higher score after turn 25 wins. Capturing the enemy Base wins at once.

toolsAdded.name: get_rules
toolsAdded.description: The rules, the constants and the whole map. Call it once, on turn 1.

toolsAdded.name: get_state
toolsAdded.description: The turn as your seat can see it: the score, what you have left to spend, the hexes you know, last turn.

toolsAdded.name: scout
toolsAdded.description: One action point for a hex and the hexes touching it, as they stood when the turn opened.

toolsAdded.name: simulate
toolsAdded.description: What your orders would do, worked out on what you know. Changes nothing.

toolsAdded.name: submit_orders
toolsAdded.description: The orders to play this turn, with your intent and your prediction of the enemy.

toolsAdded.name: read_notes
toolsAdded.description: What your seat last wrote to itself.

toolsAdded.name: write_notes
toolsAdded.description: Replace what your seat writes to itself. Notes outlive the turn.

Let me analyze the map. I'm Player B at J6. Enemy at B6.

My base J6 has 5 troops, produces 2. Nodes near me: J1 (node), D3 (node, enemy side), F6 (center node), H6 (node), H9 (node), B11 (node). Let me list nodes:
- J1 (node) - near me, top right area
- D3 (node) - enemy side
- F6 (node) - center
- D6 (node) - enemy side
- H6 (node) - near me
- H9 (node) - middle-right
- B11 (node) - enemy corner

Under half-turn rotation symmetry: B6 center maps to J6. Nodes: D3 rotates to ... let me think. Actually nodes: J1, D3, D6, F6, H6, H9, B11. That's 7 nodes. My side (B) nodes: J1 (two from base? J6 to J1 distance... J6->J5->J4->J3->J2->J1, that's far). Hmm wait "one Node two hexes from its Base and two more between three and five hexes out."

For player B base J6: node two hexes away? J6 neighbors: K6,K5,J5,I6,I7,J7. Two hexes out would be neighbors of those. Hmm, no node at two hexes from J6 directly... Let me check. Actually H6 is node: J6->I6->H6 = two hexes. Yes! H6 is a node two hexes from J6. Good.

D6 is node... that's enemy's. Wait under rotation, D6 (two from B6: B6->C6->D6) rotates to H6 (two from J6). Yes.

J1: distance from J6? J6->J5->J4->J3->J2->J1 = 5 hexes. Hmm, or J6->K6->K5->K4->K3->K2->K1->J1. J1 is 5 from J6 via J column? J6,J5,J4,J3,J2,J1 = 5 steps. That's between 3 and 5. Good.

H9: J6->I6->H6->G6... no. J6->I7->H7->H8->H9? I7 neighbor H7, H7 neighbor H8, H8 neighbor H9. That's 4 steps. Good, between 3 and 5.

F6 center.

Also B11 rotates to J1? B11 is node in enemy corner. Rotating... let's not worry.

Enemy nodes: D3 (3 from B6: B6->C6->... hmm). Actually D3, D6, B11.

Wait let me recount nodes relevant: the 7 nodes are J1, D3, F6, D6, H6, H9, B11. Enemy side nodes (near B6): D3, D6, B11. My side: J1, H6, H9. Center F6. Yes symmetric: D3<->H9, D6<->H6, B11<->J1.

So my three nodes: H6 (2 hexes), H9 (4 hexes), J1 (5 hexes).

Total hexes 91. Score: I start with 1 (base), enemy 1.

Plan: This is a greedy opponent likely. Let me think about the overall strategy. 25 turns, 6 AP each.

Key: Nodes worth 3 points, plus produce 1/turn. Bases produce 2/turn.

Strategy: Expand to capture nodes and hexes. Grab H6 early (2 hexes out). It has garrison 3. To take a neutral node, need to exceed garrison. So need 4 troops to take with 3 lost(leaves 1). Actually: "A force entering a neutral Node must exceed its garrison, and loses that many troops." So 4 troops -> lose 3, 1 remains. Then need to hold.

Initial base 5 troops, produce 2. Turn 1 I have 5 at J6.

Let me think about the opening. Move 5 from J6 to I6? Or split.

Actually taking H6: need a force of 4 arriving. J6->I6 (turn1), I6->H6 (turn2) with 4 troops. Then it becomes mine. Alternatively move 5 to I6 turn 1, then 5 to H6 turn 2, losing 3, leaving... wait combat: first fight in hex vs garrison. Actually order: arrive, then fight in hex vs enemies, then take neutral nodes. H6 is neutral node with garrison 3. Force of 5 exceeds 3, loses 3, 2 remain. So H6 captured with 2 troops.

But also I want to expand to plain hexes for points and to create supply chains.

Supply: only hexes connected to base through my own hexes score. So I need a contiguous chain.

Let me think initial: J6 has 5. I produce 2 at end of each turn. 

Actually, I should be careful about expansion speed. Let me consider moving all 5 out turn 1 to I6. Then J6 empty but owned, produces 2 at end (base production is per base regardless? "Each Base gains 2 troops" - yes base produces regardless of troops, ownership keeps). Actually the base produces 2 each turn as long as I own it. Since I own J6 even when emptied ("A hex stays yours when its last troop leaves").

Hmm but leaving base empty is risky if enemy reaches it—but they're far.

Turn 1: Move 5 J6->I6. Now I6 has 5. J6 produces 2 -> J6 has 2.

Turn 2: I6 5 troops. Move 5 I6->H6 to take node? That leaves I6 empty. H6 captured with 2. Or move to H6 and also expand elsewhere.

Alternatively, split: some to take H6, some toward J1/J5 etc.

Let me think about what gives best points. Hexes worth 1 each, nodes 3. Supply matters.

Actually a strong opening: expand along a broad front to claim many plain hexes cheaply (they have no garrison; neutral plain hexes—do they need troops? "Take neutral Nodes" only nodes have garrisons. Plain neutral hexes: just move in a single troop to claim? A hex with surviving troops belongs to you. So moving 1 troop into a neutral plain hex claims it). So plain hexes cost 1 troop each to claim.

Wait but do neutral plain hexes have garrison? The rules say node_garrison 3, and taking neutral Nodes requires exceeding garrison. Plain hexes presumably have 0 garrison. Moving troops into a neutral plain hex: step 5 "Fight in the hex. Where both players have troops, or one enters a hex the other owns" - not the case for neutral. Step 6 take neutral Nodes - not a node. Step 7 set ownership - troops present => mine. So yes, 1 troop claims a plain hex.

So expansion: spread 1 troop to each adjacent plain neutral hex to claim it. But I only have 5 troops and 6 AP.

Turn 1: from J6 I can move to K6, K5, J5, I6, I7, J7. Six neighbors. With 5 troops and 6 AP, I can send 1 to five of them (or fewer).

But sending single troops out leaves them vulnerable and doesn't build a strike force. However claiming hexes gives points and supply.

content.text:
The match is over. Here's my summary of the game as Seat B:

**Result:** Loss — final score roughly **39–51** in favor of the enemy (Player A).

**What went well:**
- Fast, broad expansion early (scores 4→7→15→20→26→31→36), grabbing the F-column plus my home hexes.
- Captured three nodes: **H6** (T3), **H9** (T11), and **J1** (T16), giving me a production base.
- Momentarily retook the central node **F6** on T14.

**What went wrong:**
- The enemy filled its whole half faster and reached the contested **F-column and center** first.
- Repeated 4-stack contests over **F6** ended in mutual destruction; the enemy eventually took and entrenched it (stack grew to 7–14), giving them a 4th node and a permanent production edge.
- They then pushed into my own half (G3, G4, G5, H3, H5), so I spent the late game trading single hexes back and forth instead of gaining.

**Decisive factor:** node production. Holding F6 from ~turn 13 let the enemy out-produce me while my repeated failed F6 assaults burned 4 troops each time.

**Lessons for next time:** commit to the central node earlier with a decisive stack, and avoid grinding equal 4-vs-4 attacks into it; value production tempo over marginal hex-grabbing.
